title: Getting Out of Trump’s Wars
text:
Subscribe here: Apple Podcasts | Spotify | YouTube | Overcast | Pocket Casts 

 Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth survived a congressional impeachment attempt last week, but oversight of Hegseth will be one of the new Congress’s most pressing tasks. Though Hegseth’s management of the war in Iran—a war that has now passed its eighth month without a constitutionally mandated congressional declaration—is his most glaring failure, the politicization of the Pentagon, the purging of qualified generals, and the targeted, extrajudicial killing of noncombatants all demand investigation and debate.

 In this episode of Autocracy in America , Representative Jason Crow talks about what form congressional oversight of the military should take. Crow sits on the House’s Armed Services and Intelligence Committees.

 The following is a transcript of the episode: 

 Anne Applebaum: I’m Anne Applebaum. In this season of the Autocracy in America podcast, we’re asking how to undo the damage the Trump presidencies have now done to our political system, and how to reverse the slide to autocracy, even as Trump himself remains in office.

 In modern times, no U.S. president has politicized and personalized the military more than Donald Trump. During his first term, he told his then chief of staff, John Kelly, that he wanted to have the kind of generals that Hitler had, who would be totally loyal to him and follow orders. This instinct directly contradicts the ethos of the U.S. military, whose officers are trained to be loyal to the American Constitution and not to a particular politician or party.

 In his second term, Trump has done his best to establish a more autocratic ethos inside the military. He appointed Pete Hegseth, a Fox News host with no major organizational experience, to be secretary of defense. Hegseth, using opaque, informal criteria, immediately began firing qualified, experienced senior military leaders who just happened to be female or Black.

 He then continued to purge respected, talented officers, often with no public explanation. Since January 2025, Trump and Hegseth have taken the U.S. military even farther away from their traditions. They ordered strikes on fishing boats allegedly carrying drugs, a form of extrajudicial murder. They launched a war on Iran unprovoked, causing civilian casualties and damaging U.S. bases in the Gulf to a degree that has still not been fully accounted for or explained to the public.

 Trump even involved the Pentagon in a murky transaction in Venezuela, drawing the military into what may be a corrupt relationship with the Chavista regime, now led by Delcy Rodríguez.

 To talk about Trump’s attempt to transform the culture of the U.S. military into something recognizably autocratic, I’ve invited Jason Crow, congressman from Colorado.

 Congressman Crow is a veteran of the 82nd Airborne Division and the 75th Ranger Regiment, and he fought in Iraq and Afghanistan.

 [ Music ] 

 He serves on both intelligence and armed services committees in the House and will be one of those investigating the abuse of the military. Congressman Jason Crow, thanks for joining us.

 Jason Crow: Thank you, Anne.

 Applebaum: We’ve already had one failed attempt to impeach Pete Hegseth. Will there be another? And why does it matter? What do you think impeachment can achieve?

 Crow: Yeah, it’s a great question, Anne, about: Are we gonna impeach Hegseth? And I remind folks that impeachment is just a tool. It’s not an end in and of itself, right? It’s a tool. There are many tools Congress has available to achieve its goals. So we actually have to start with: What is the goal? And the goal, for me, is to get Pete Hegseth removed as the head of the Department of Defense.

 Because every day he sits atop the DOD is a day that our service members don’t have the leadership, they don’t have the competency, they don’t have the direction and the support that they need, and they are being put at great risk. So removing Hegseth is the goal. Impeachment is one of the ways to do that, and I won’t hesitate to pursue impeachment if I think it’s the way to achieve that.

 Applebaum: But will the impeachment process address some of the deeper harms that he’s done? For example, the politicization of the military—the fact that Hegseth fired or removed very senior generals and commanders apparently for reasons that had nothing to do with merit, that were to do with whether they were so-called DEI hires, whether they were Black, whether they were women. Is there any way to fix or go back or reexamine any of that?

 Crow: You don’t fix those things via impeachment. You can discover those things in an impeachment investigation, in an impeachment proceeding and trial, of which I am very familiar ’cause I was an impeachment prosecutor in the first impeachment of Donald Trump, so I know a lot about the process.

 There is a fact-finding, investigative aspect of impeachment, and then that goes for ultimate—a trial for conviction in the Senate. But you don’t fix those things through impeachment. So we’re gonna embark on an investigative and fact-finding process. We have created, under the Armed Services Committee—or we’re about to create; we’ve already publicized this—a new subcommittee called the Oversight and Investigation Subcommittee, where we’re gonna put a lot of the investigations into that subcommittee, and we’re gonna start that in January.

 And then in addition to that, our other subcommittees of jurisdiction—the personnel, the readiness, the tactical land and sea forces—those are all gonna do their own investigations.

 The point is not just to do an investigation. The point, Anne, per your question, is to actually discover the information, because the last two years, our ability to get information has fallen off a cliff.

 They have stonewalled; they have refused to answer; they’ve refused to brief us. There’s so many things we don’t know that we have to learn.

 Applebaum: Let me also ask what you and your committee, and Congress more broadly, can do about stopping or forcing a negotiation to end the war in Iran.

I know there are some deeper issues about whether the president defied Congress to start it. Will Congress have the ability to change how it’s fought? Will we learn more about the damage done to U.S. bases and U.S. interests in the region?

 Crow: Well, we’ve now taken votes, and these are in the form of resolutions to end the war in Iran. So we actually have a standing resolution that has passed that says that the president must end the war. And when we retake the majority, we will have more options to look at how do we enforce that resolution.

 But the more powerful tool, and probably the more viable tool, is funding. We can just cut the funding off, and I do not buy this argument at all that when you break it, you buy it—that we just have to continue to throw good money after bad. That’s what we did for years in Iraq and Afghanistan. We heard some variation of this argument: that we have to continue to do it, because one more troop surge, one more new strategy, one new general or admiral with a new idea about how to prosecute the war is somehow gonna fix it. Or, you know, escalation is the way out.

 We spent $3 trillion, 7,000 American lives, hundreds of thousands of lives wounded. We want out. Americans want out. That was the message last Tuesday.

 They don’t want this endless cycle of conflict anymore. So yeah, we can cut it off and direct the military to wind down operations, and that’s my intent.

 Applebaum: And so you would just say in a budget resolution, “We don’t fund this,” and then the money doesn’t go. Is it that simple and that straightforward?

 Crow: It’s not as straightforward as that. We have an appropriations process that we’re starting in January, so a budgeting process. We have to look at the ongoing budget. How do we detract money from those functions, right? So you have to figure out, and this is part of the fact-finding process and why fact-finding is so important, because: How are you paying for this? What units are deploying and when? Those are all the essential questions we have to ask and the answers we need to get, so then we can figure out: How do we budget that to make sure that we are peeling out the critical national security functions that have to happen, that have to continue, and we’re not impacting those operations, but we are properly carving out Iran war operations and winding down that funding?

 Applebaum: And will this process begin to return power to Congress over warfare, which is what Congress is meant to have?

 Crow: It’s a great first step, right? I think the story of the moment we’ve been in the last two years is a story of the height of presidential power in America and the low point of congressional power in American history.

 We have to correct that, and it starts with appropriations in January, but we also have to revisit the authorizations for use of military force, these AUMFs that are being used as blank checks now for military operations. And that’s not to say that we shouldn’t use the military to keep ourselves safe, to combat terrorism, to support our allies.

 That’s not what I’m saying. But what I am saying is these AUMFs that have been on the books for over 20 years now without debate, without reauthorization, and without appropriation. They’re funded largely by debt funding at this point. They have to end.

 And no Congress should occur—there shouldn’t be any two-year period where the people’s elected representatives aren’t forced to debate and vote on these.

 Applebaum: Let me now turn to a slightly different subject but one that’s related, which is the military’s attacks on fishing boats allegedly carrying drugs. These were attacks that you could describe as extrajudicial murder: using the military to attack civilian targets.

 Maybe they were carrying drugs. Maybe they weren’t. There was no process to find out. People were killed, and famously on one occasion, people may even have been killed by a second strike—survivors of a first strike—by an American missile or an American bomb. Is that something that Congress can force the military to take responsibility for? Is it something that we can hold them accountable for?

 Crow: Absolutely, and it’s near the top of my list. I’ve heard some people say these are war crimes. There’s no war. There’s no declaration of war—

 Applebaum : Exactly.

 Crow : —so they’re not war crimes, which actually just makes these, if they are what they appear to be, murder.

 If there’s no war, and you have no self-defense argument—which in some of these cases is very clear to me. I’ve actually seen the video. I’ve seen the video of one of the most disturbing strikes, one of the very first ones in September of 2025, which seemed very clear to me to be folks who have been taken off the battlefield—so to speak, using the military terminology—that pose no risk to any military service member.

 And a second strike was ordered that resulted in the death of these individuals, which, as a former military commander, there is no justification that I can see in that strike for taking it. And so there needs to be accountability. We need to actually reinvigorate rule of law in America, so we can not let these things pass. We have to stop these operations as an initial matter and then seek accountability if there are violations—or criminal violations, in some cases—that may have occurred.

 Applebaum: And in a situation like that, who is responsible? Is it the military commander who gave the order to give the strike, or is it again the secretary of defense? Is it Pete Hegseth?

 Crow: Well, the answer is yes. The answer is everybody. Right? Which is why the group of us, me, Mark Kelly, Elissa Slotkin, filmed a video last November—about a year ago this week, I think, actually, when we released the video—where we reminded our service members that they have an obligation to follow the Constitution, the rule of law, to follow lawful orders, but they have a similar obligation to not follow, to disobey unlawful orders.

 And everybody along the chain of command has that obligation, from the very senior person ordering the operation to the person pulling the trigger.

 Applebaum: And almost immediately after that, Pete Hegseth tried to have you arrested, correct?

 Crow: Well, the president first—he first said he was gonna have us executed, and then tried, actually in that order. So he even screwed the order up. And then he directed the Department of Justice to attempt to indict us not once, but twice in February of this year. Of course, they failed in that. But yeah, another clear example of the weaponization of America’s Department of Justice to go after Donald Trump’s perceived political enemies.

 Applebaum: Is there any precedent for that that you know of in American history? Is that the first time it’s happened?

 Crow: Where sitting members of Congress were—

 Applebaum: Accused ...

 Crow: —that they tried to put ’em in prison for reminding people to follow the Constitution? I can’t think of a precedent for that. ( Laughs .) If you don’t know the precedent, Anne, I don’t think anybody would actually. Why are you asking me this? You know more about this than I do.

 ( Both laugh .)

 Applebaum: No, actually, you know how the Army deals with these kinds of issues better than me. I mean, you were a commander, so you would know.

 Crow: I do.

 [ Break ] 

 Applebaum: One of the very odd things that’s happened in the last year that hasn’t had that much attention has been the Pentagon’s involvement in what could be a very corrupt oil deal in Venezuela.

 Last August, the Trump administration announced there would be this fantastic deal between the U.S. government, and technically an office in the Pentagon, and a Venezuelan company that’s led by a very famous crony of the Chavista regime. And there are all kinds of oddities about the deal.

 It’s unclear who the real owners are. The company is based in Barbados. The deal seems to be set up to give lots of opportunities for cronies on both sides, really, to take part in the process. Is that in your remit, and is that something Congress can also look at? And would it have the power to stop?

 Crow: It falls squarely in our jurisdiction, and it’s a really important issue that we’re going to investigate, because it goes to the type of corruption that Americans said they want to stop, and they want us to stop it, to investigate and to stop it. That was the very clear message, right?

 ’Cause corruption, actually for the first time in my life, was an essential kitchen-table issue that Americans voted on. It was one of the top three issues in polls, in surveys, and my many hundreds of discussions with thousands of voters. This has been a remarkable story about the role of free press in a democratic society because the press has really stepped up in a remarkable way.

 And I read your piece about this Venezuelan oil deal recently, Anne. Remarkable journalism and investigation. And then what that does is that helps highlight things that Americans deserve answers to, because hundreds of millions of dollars of taxpayer money that should be allocated to the health and welfare of our troops, to military housing, to drones, to all these new-generation systems that we need to keep Americans safe are being siphoned off to rackets like this.

 Applebaum: I think you told me that when you were on the campaign trail you were surprised to hear how many people were talking about the president’s ballroom,

 because the ballroom was a kind of symbol of excess and a symbol of the way in which the corruption was out of hand.

 Crow: Yeah. This is one of the reasons why I think, Anne, that corruption has become a kitchen-table issue. I oftentimes am asked, usually in TV interviews, they’re like, “What are you gonna do? Are you gonna do oversight or anti-corruption stuff, or are you gonna do kitchen-table stuff?”

 And I say, “Listen, you don’t get it. Corruption is a kitchen-table issue now.” There’s billions of taxpayer money—that’s money that should be going to health care, should be going to help people buy homes, should be going to education. That’s going in the pockets of the Trump family and their cronies and campaign donors.

 And it’s wrong. So absolutely people have seen this and the tangible aspect of it, right? What has happened is it’s been so tangible, it’s been so rank and so obvious, and it contrasts so significantly with what Americans are going through. I often, throughout the campaign cycle, would get some variation of this.

 They’re like, “Wow, they get a gold ballroom and I can’t pay my health-care premiums anymore.” You know: “Kristi Noem gets a brand-new fleet of private planes, I’m closing my restaurant next week.” Right? “They get an arch, and my ranch is going under.”

 So that is the contrast that Americans see right now, and that is a big reason why it’s become a kitchen-table issue.

 Applebaum: One of the things the Venezuelan deal said to me, though, was that we might also need—aside from investigation of what’s happened in the past—new laws or new rules.

 I was amazed that this was even legal, that an office in the Pentagon can take part in effectively a joint venture to drill for oil in Venezuela. I mean, how is that even possible? Do we need to rethink what’s allowed and what’s not allowed? A lot of things that the president seems to do appear to be legal, but immoral.

 And it feels like maybe the old norms or the old assumptions about what the president is or isn’t allowed to do need to be updated.

 Crow: I think it’s both. We have a lot of laws in the books that historically have worked. One of the greatest anti-corruption laws in the history of America—in the history of the world, really—is the Foreign Corrupt Practices Act.

 The FCPA, which has been in the books I think since the early ’70s, has done remarkable work of cleaning up international business practices. Now, it hasn’t solved the problem, clearly, but things are significantly better now than they were before the FCPA was in the books.

 This administration has actually stopped in whole enforcing the FCPA, so we need to pick back up. We need to enforce the laws that are on the books, and we clearly need to close loopholes and pass additional laws to address the things that are very clearly not in the spirit of the law and not consistent with our country’s values.

 Applebaum: Let me ask you about one other strange thing that’s happened in the last year, is that we’ve seen the Pentagon effectively ceding more and more power to Elon Musk. His companies are so important now to the U.S. military that it’s effectively giving him decision-making process over U.S. foreign policy. And we saw this in the system that’s used by Ukrainian troops to defend themselves against Russian drones.

 Is that also something that’s in the purview of Congress? Can you also begin to look at the unusual amount of power that this one person has?

 Crow: Yeah, absolutely. I have yet to meet any American, Republican, Democrat, or independent, who wants a private, unelected tech oligarch to be in charge of a key national-security system and to be able to make decisions like this.

 Like, who in their right mind thinks this is okay and a good idea? It’s clearly not. So that is squarely within our purview. And there’s a couple of things happening that we need to unravel. One is this general dynamic of large defense companies that have that much power, that much control, that have become so essential that we just can’t operate without them.

 There shouldn’t be any one person or company that has that much influence that we are that reliant upon. And that’s an indictment, frankly—and I say that colloquially. ( Laughs .) I can’t use that word these days. I have to be very clear. That’s an indictment of our procurement and acquisition system, right?

 Which favors these small number of very large, powerful companies, which—as we see in the Ukraine war right now—are actually doing us a disservice, because a lot of the innovation, a lot of the incredible work that’s happening in Ukraine that’s generating the future of warfare right now, is these small, disaggregated, hundreds of different companies that are innovating and evolving rapidly.

 So that’s number one.

 Number two: the incompetence of the Pete Hegseth Department of Defense, which allows this to happen, ’cause they’re checked out.

 Number three is the lack of engagement by the president. He’s just not engaged half the time and not interested and just allows things to happen, which then means that the private sector and these tech oligarchs do whatever they want.

 And then number four: the lack of oversight and accountability for the company.

 So it’s really those four issues kind of converging to create a massive problem for our national security.

 Applebaum: What exactly does that look like? What does control over Elon Musk mean?

 Crow: Well, the first step is we have to get the answers to figure out what happened.

 Was there a violation of law sometime, somewhere along the sequence? Or was it just something that happened because that’s how we’re structured, and we’ve given the keys to the castle to a private citizen?

 Those are two different situations. But what is clear is that there is a role for Congress to look holistically at the amount of power that we’re giving private citizens—unelected tech company CEOs—to our critical national-security systems, and the ability of those folks to make decisions without oversight, without accountability, and presumably without our government even knowing about it.

 Now, I’m suspicious that folks didn’t know about it. I think people did, and I wanna know who knew about it. But piecing together that chronology and figuring out what were the points of failure at every step, and how do we close those gaps legislatively or through appropriations or through restructuring our National Security Council or agencies to make sure that we put stopgaps in place.

 Applebaum: Or restructuring Starlink.

 Crow: Yeah, that too.

 Applebaum: It’s connected to another issue that I alluded to at the beginning. I think looks like the Pentagon was very surprised at the beginning of the Iran war by the Iranian regime’s ability to use drones to hit U.S. bases.

 And I’ve heard people close to the Pentagon or in that world worry that the U.S. isn’t innovating enough, that we don’t have a plan for how to protect our very large, very expensive assets, our ships, our planes, our bases, against very cheap drones of the kind that are being used in the Ukraine war.

 And so there’s a question as to whether we’re even learning the lessons of the Ukraine war. I mean, the Ukrainians are begging to show them to us and want to help us, and are very happy to share technology, and at least until now, we have been pushing it away, presumably because of the president’s prejudice against Ukraine and in favor of the Russians. Is that your impression?

 Crow: Yeah, absolutely. First of all, the president’s animus toward Ukraine is, you know—the man operates largely by personal grievance. That’s how he makes policy, if you can even call it that. That’s how he makes decisions. Most of what they do, 90-plus percent, is either corruption—they’re either monetizing the federal government and trying to make as much money as possible off the backs of the American people—or vengeance, settling scores.

 That’s most of what they do, or explains most of what they do, I should say. But it’s not just that we’re not learning the lesson for Ukraine. We legally aren’t even structured the right way. I go back to the least sexy topic ever, and that is defense procurement and acquisition reform.

 Applebaum: ( Laughs. )

 Crow: But the most important topic right now, right?

 Because lawfully, legally, we actually cannot do what they’re doing in Ukraine. And I know you’ve seen this. You’ve written about it; you’ve seen this firsthand and have studied it. The innovation cycle is a weekly cycle now. They’re fielding systems; they’re learning on the battlefield in Ukraine, and even Iran is doing this, and then they’re rapidly iterating within a matter of days or weeks.

 Legally, our system won’t allow that to happen, ’cause you gotta put out bids. You have to do contract. You have to do testing. You have to do evaluation. So we are legally not structured to allow that to happen. That’s number one.

 Number two is we’ve bifurcated our procurement from the war-fighting function.

 So it’s the services, Army, Navy, Air Force, Marine Corps, which actually don’t do war-fighting. They exist to field and build the forces, and then they loan those forces to our combatant commands, but they’re the ones that are actually fielding all of our systems. And then the combatant commands are the ones that do the fighting.

 How in God’s name can we iterate and evolve rapidly when our war fighters and our commanders, who are actually on the ground, have no part in the fielding and our acquisition system? It’s crazy. So we have to merge those functions.

 Applebaum: And that’s something you’ll also hear from Congress in the next two years?

 You’ll hear—

 Crow: Absolutely ...

 Applebaum: —pressure to do that. Let me ask you about one final thing, which is something I know you know about, because we talked about it when you were in Warsaw a few weeks ago, which is U.S. allies. So we’re in a really strange position, whereas if there were a general or an admiral joining this conversation and we were to ask them about American alliances, they would say, “Well, of course we exercise with our allies. All of our military plans include our allies. We think about the future of NATO; we think about the future of the Pacific alliances as a kind of fundamental part of what we do.” And you have that, and then on the other hand, you have the White House—the president—verbally attacking allies.

 You have members of the administration talking about pulling out of NATO, or at least pulling troops out of Europe, that might even be part of the negotiations that have been going on between Russia and Ukraine in recent weeks. What do you say now to allies, and what will Congress’s role be in grappling with this question?

 Because this going forward is something that the outside world is watching really closely.

 Crow: Well, the first thing is a recognition that—when we were in Warsaw, for example, meeting with a lot of my fellow parliamentarians and ministers, what’s clear is that all of us, to some degree, are dealing with dynamics, similar dynamics, right?

 We’re all dealing with the rise of far-right movements. We’re all dealing with the impacts on our society of information change and aggregation and social media and AI. We’re all dealing with the political and economic ramifications of mass migration on our societies, which are driving many of our domestic political challenges.

 We’re all dealing with economic insolvency to some degree. I mean, you don’t have to go far in Europe to talk to somebody who says that their country’s broken—or broke, rather. There’s nothing that we can really say.

 I can’t say anything that’s gonna allay people’s concerns or is gonna say America is back, ’cause they’ve heard it before. They’ve heard us say that before. We just actually have to show them. There are concrete steps that we have to take to show folks.

 And then the third is the importance, really the critical importance, of subnational diplomacy, and I think this is key. As we look at trying to reshape new alliances, America’s new role in the world, which is gonna look different than it—we’re not going back. We’re not trying to rebuild what once was. We’re gonna try to build a new alliance network that’s gonna operate differently, is subnational diplomacy, to even out those highs and lows of all the national levels. ’Cause in the United States and Paris, and in London they have these too, right?

 So the key is: How do we piece together, in a stronger way, the civic organizations, the NGOs, the members of Congress with the parliamentarians, the sister-city programs, the state-partnership exchange programs, the state National Guard military-assistance programs, all of these things that continue, in a more even way that really make up the connective tissue of relationships in foreign policy?

 So I wanna double and triple down on that subnational level to really show that we can have consistent and meaningful engagement regardless of who’s in the White House.

 Applebaum: So you’re saying that there’s a danger that the alliances became hollowed out—that it was just sort of people at the top talking—and that what we need is a revival of more, as you say, democratic and civic links between countries that are closely related?

 Crow: Yeah. I mean, that is a more succinct way. ( Laughs. ) We need more doers. We just need to do more stuff that’s meaningful and actually delivers for our people. Foreign policy and national security, all of it, every function, including our alliances, should do two things. It should keep constituents safe. And it should make sure that life is better for Americans. Aid, human rights, rule of law, all of those flow into those two goals.

 We’re nowhere near a post-American world. This is my opinion. Certainly in Europe, right? It’s debatable in other places what our role is, but certainly in Europe we’re nowhere near a post-American world, and they will rely on us and we will rely on them far into the future.

 Applebaum: Yeah, I hope that you go on explaining to your constituents that the American relationship with Europe is something that’s of benefit to both sides. It’s not a cost to the United States, as the president sometimes likes to say. It produces trade links; it produces prosperity; it produces peace; it produces the possibility of travel and exchange that wouldn’t exist otherwise.

 Crow: Absolutely. And I point that out that Ukraine aid is not charity, actually. This is an investment we’re making in ourselves, in our industrial base, in our partnerships. And Ukraine has now become the largest provider of security on the continent of Europe. They are now a security guarantor for the United States and for NATO.

 When we invest in that, we are investing in a security provider for the rest of the continent. And if we can help Ukraine be successful, which we must, then we’ll have the largest, most sophisticated, most battle-tested military on the continent of Europe that’s allied with us, that’s our friend and our trading partner, that will help keep Russia and Vladimir Putin at bay.

 And that’s a hell of a deal.

 Applebaum: I’m delighted to end with that. Thank you so much, Congressman Jason Crow.

 Crow: Thank you, Anne.
